whatItIs.text: A chemical leavener — bicarbonate plus acid salts, kept apart by cornstarch — that releases carbon dioxide when wetted (and again when heated, if double-acting).

historyNote.text: The first commercial baking powder was Borwick's, launched in England in 1842 after eleven years of perfecting a chemist's formula; the double-acting kind followed in 1860s America, making quick breads — and modern cakes and biscuits — possible.

howToChoose.text: Choose double-acting tins (most are) and check the date; a tin that has been open a year may still work — test a spoonful in hot water, which should fizz hard.

storage.text: Keep the tin tightly sealed in a dry cupboard; moisture is what sets it off.

foodSafetyRef.note: Practice storage guidance only; no rulebook content is claimed. The app's food-safety rules live in data/food-safety/rules.json.

useItUp.text: Half-empty tins still leaven pancakes and scones; for the truly stale, the tin's bicarbonate fraction makes a fine fridge deodoriser — but buy fresh for baking.

substitutions.ratio: 1/4 tsp soda + 1/2 tsp tartar per tsp powder
